n9aeab6436516: Background: Connexin 43 (Cx43) gap junctions are abnormally accumulated and lateralized in Atrial fibrillation (AF), however, the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. The purpose of this study is to explore the role of optineurin (OPTN), a selective autophagy receptor, in maintaining Cx43 homeostasis and protecting against AF. Methods: Firstly, three publicly available AF-related datasets were analyzed to evaluate the potential relationship of OPTN with AF. Then, to examine whether OPTN-mediated selective autophagy is involved in regulating the fate of Cx43 in AF, Co-IP and immunofluorescence staining were used to determine Cx43/LC3B/OPTN colocalization; 3-MA (autophagy inhibitor) and MG132 (proteasome inhibitor) were used to check the Cx43 degradation pathway in AC-16/H9C2 cells, which underwent programmed electrical stimulation (1 Hz, 10 V, 4 ms, 24 h). Finally, rats with AAV-mediated OPTN overexpression and autophagy regulators were used to detect the effect of OPTN-mediated autophagy on the expression and distribution of Cx43 in AF. Results: OPTN was downregulated in AF (datasets and patient tissues), accompanied by a decrease in LC3B-II/I and an increase in p62. Co-IP confirmed OPTN-Cx43 binding. In OPTN-overexpressing H9C2 cells, MG132 treatment failed to change Cx43 expression level, whereas inhibition of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway by 3-MA led to marked accumulation of Cx43. OPTN overexpression promoted the colocalization of Cx43 with LC3, whereas opposite results were observed in cardiomyocytes transfected with OPTN-specific siRNA. In AF rats, autophagy activation or OPTN overexpression reduced heart weight/body weight ratio, AF duration, left atrial enlargement, structural disorganization, fibrosis, Cx43 lateralization, apoptosis, and oxidative stress. Concurrently, these treatments improved conduction time, conduction velocity, conduction heterogeneity, and AF susceptibility. Conclusions: OPTN-mediated selective autophagy has an important effect on reducing pathological accumulation and abnormal distribution of Cx43 in AF, which provides new mechanistic insights and potential therapeutic targets for AF. na8d73162e75f: Background: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, a manifestation of the metabolic syndrome affects around 38% of Americans. It is associated with a higher risk for cardiovascular disease (CVD) events-i.e., acute myocardial infarction (AMI), congestive heart failure (CHF), and ischemic stroke. Fibrosis-4 Index (FIB-4) is calculated using aminotransferases [aspartate (AST) and alanine (ALT)], and platelets [FIB-4 =(Age x AST)/(Platelets x √ALT). It assesses advanced fibrosis risk in patients with chronic liver disease. FIB-4 has been shown to have an association with CVD events but is not utilized as a predictor of CVD outcomes in clinical practice. We wanted to understand the additional predictive information of FIB-4 beyond traditional CVD risk indicators and how this association varies over time, while controlling for cardiometabolic therapies like statins, insulin, metformin, glucagon like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1a). Methods: This is a retrospective cohort study of electronic health record data from a national cohort of Veterans, extracted from the VA Corporate Data Warehouse. Veterans with calculable FIB-4 scores from January 2011 to December 2025 were identified, and excluded if CVD event occurred before 2011. FIB-4 scores were categorized as low (FIB-4 <1.3), indeterminate (1.3 ≤ FIB-4 <2.67), or high-risk (FIB-4 ≥ 2.67) for advanced fibrosis. We used multivariable complementary log-log (cloglog) regression models to evaluate the association between FIB-4 scores and other potential confounders and covariates with time to composite CVD event outcome (AMI, CHF, and stroke). Results: A total of 2,431,410 unique patients were identified. Approximately 45% of patients were 64 years of age or older, male (93.5%), and White (73.9%). Among this cohort, 43% had diabetes mellitus, 24% had chronic kidney disease (CKD), and 24.2% had severe liver disease (SLD). During a mean follow-up of 10.23 years, patients with FIB-4 scores at high- (HR=1.26; 95% CI [1.25 - 1.27]) or indeterminate-risk (HR=1.26; 95% CI [1.09 - 1.1.09 - 1.10]) for advanced fibrosis were more likely to experience a CVD event compared to those with low-risk FIB-4 scores. Other factors associated with an elevated hazard for CVD events included CKD (HR=1.58; 95%CI [1.57 - 1.59]), SLD (HR=1.31; 95%CI [1.30 - 1.33]), prescription for insulin (HR=1.94; 95% CI [1.93 - 1.96]) and statin (HR=2.02; 95% CI [2.01 - 2.03]). Alternatively, a prescription for GLP-1a and metformin had an associated 19% (HR=0.81; 95% CI [1.93 - 1.96]) and 12% (HR=0.88; 95%CI [0.87 - 0.89]) reduction of CVD event hazard, respectively. Conclusions: In a large cohort of Veterans from primary care, FIB-4 scores at high- and indeterminate-risk for advanced fibrosis were associated with an increased risk of incident CVD over time. The utility of adding FIB-4 components to future CVD risk prognostication requires further exploration.
n8f04b7917384: Introduction: Anthracyclines such as doxorubicin (Dox) are highly effective chemotherapeutic agents that treat a variety of malignancies, but their use is limited by dose-dependent cardiotoxic effects. While specific immune cell types have been implicated in the pathogenesis of cardiotoxicity, a comprehensive understanding of the immune landscape of Dox cardiomyopathy is lacking. Methods: Wild-type mice were treated with either saline or low-dose Dox (3 mg/kg x 8 intraperitoneally), a regimen that replicates delayed cardiomyopathy seen in patients. CD45+ cardiac immune cells were isolated using magnetic-activated cell sorting. CITE-seq was used to map the cardiac immune composition within the tissue. The top 500 differentially expressed genes between saline-treated and Dox-treated hearts were further investigated using mouse and human plasma proteomics. Flow cytometry and ELISA were further used to validate findings in mice with Dox cardiomyopathy. Results: Nineteen distinct immune cell clusters were identified in mouse hearts treated with saline or Dox. Dox increased both the number and proportion of cardiac neutrophils, macrophages, monocytes, NK cells, dendritic cells, and T-cells. Several of these populations were validated by flow cytometry, and remained increased at a chronic time point. Differential gene analysis across immune cell types revealed an increase in both pro-inflammatory genes and pro-repair mediators in Dox-treated hearts. We compared these top genes to the plasma proteome of mice treated with Dox and found 48 to be similarly changed after correction for false discovery rate, suggesting overlap between the cardiac and systemic immune response. We then looked for matching proteins in the plasma proteome from lymphoma patients treated with anthracyclines and found 3 proteins to be associated with early cardiac toxicity: IGFBP-3 (R=-0.4, p=0.01), IGFBP-7 (R=-0.35, p=0.03), and IEX1 (R=-0.37, p=0.02). Validation by ELISA showed correlation of IGFBP-3 (R=-0.38, p=0.002) and IGFBP-7 (R=-0.31, p=0.01) with Dox cardiotoxicity, both of which were expressed by highly inflammatory and pro-fibrotic leukocytes. Conclusion: This study provides novel insight into the immune response to Dox treatment. Mediators of local cardiac and systemic inflammation, such as IGFBP3/7, have the potential to serve as mechanistic biomarkers of early cardiotoxicity in patients treated with Dox.
n690f9f67aeb2: Background: BMI is an imperfect surrogate for adiposity and cardiometabolic risk. The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Commission proposed an expanded obesity definition that adds waist circumference (WC), waist-to-height ratio (WHtR), and waist-to-hip ratio (WHR) to BMI, and further distinguished preclinical obesity from clinical obesity based on the presence of organ dysfunction or functional limitation. The population distribution of individual anthropometric components, and how they differ across preclinical and clinical obesity phenotypes, remains unknown. Aim: To characterize the distribution of Lancet components and assess how each combination differs in identifying preclinical versus clinical obesity phenotypes in U.S. adults, using DXA-derived adiposity as a reference. Methods: We analyzed adults aged 20-59 years in NHANES 2017-2018 undergoing whole-body DXA. The reference standard for excess adiposity was DXA (Dual-Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry) total body fat ≥25% (men)/≥35% (women). Secondary outcomes were DXA-estimated visceral obesity (≥130 cm 2 men; ≥100 cm 2 women) and clinical obesity (Lancet obesity plus a metabolic or end-organ manifestation); participants meeting Lancet anthropometric criteria without these manifestations were classified as preclinical obesity. Participants were cross-classified into mutually exclusive combinations of the Lancet components; for each subset we estimated the survey-weighted proportion with each true outcome (the positive predictive value [PPV]) and the subset’s share of total disease burden. Results: Among 1,900 adults (≈98.7 million weighted), 69% (95% CI 67-71) had true DXA-verified excess adiposity, versus 36% (35-38) classified as obese by BMI alone. PPV for DXA-defined adiposity varied widely across combinations (Table 1). BMI≥40 kg/m 2 and BMI plus all anthropometrics carried the highest PPVs, with 100% and 96% for excess adiposity and 88% and 62% for visceral obesity, respectively. BMI+WC+WHtR (no hip metric) performed comparably (95% excess adiposity; 66% clinical obesity). In contrast, isolated WHR positivity captured only 16% with excess adiposity and 7.4% with visceral obesity. BMI plus all anthropometrics also accounted for the largest absolute share of visceral (53%) and clinical (41%) obesity (Table 2). Conclusion: The Lancet’s multi-metric components vary substantially in their distribution across preclinical and clinical obesity phenotypes. While the combination of BMI with all central and hip anthropometrics captures the highest proportion of absolute visceral and clinical obesity in the U.S. population, we found that the hip-derived WHR performs poorly alone. Simpler waist-centric combinations (BMI+WC+WHtR) achieve comparable PPVs here. Thus, implementation of the Lancet framework may have the potential to be streamlined.
nf3e963bb9017: Background: Veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) is a rescue therapy for refractory cardiac arrest and severe shock. Although cannulation strategies are standardized, decannulation decisions remain variable. When hemodynamic collapse occurs after decannulation, emergent re-cannulation may be the only life-saving option. Outcomes after a second VA-ECMO run during the same hospitalization are poorly defined, particularly among extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) patients, a group often presumed to have especially poor prognosis. Hypothesis: A second VA-ECMO run during the same hospitalization is associated with meaningful survival to discharge. Aim: To evaluate survival and predictors of outcome after repeat VA-ECMO cannulation during the same hospitalization. Methods: This is a retrospective single-center study of patients who underwent two VA-ECMO runs during a single hospitalization between 2016-2024. Among 1,000 patients treated with VA-ECMO, 40 required emergent re-initiation after initial decannulation. Clinical characteristics, indications for re-cannulation, survival to hospital discharge and predictors of outcome at the time of re-cannulation were analyzed. Results: Survival to hospital discharge after repeat VA-ECMO was 32.5% (Table 1). The most common indications for re-cannulation were refractory cardiogenic shock (52%) and cardiac arrest requiring ECPR (40%) (Table 2). Patients re-cannulated for ECPR had survival comparable to, and numerically higher than, those re-cannulated for other indications, including refractory cardiogenic shock (44% versus 24%; p=0.29). Survivors were younger and less likely to have a history of coronary artery bypass grafting (Table 1). At the time of re-cannulation, survivors had lower serum lactate, international normalized ratio levels and higher platelet counts (Table 2). On multivariable analysis, older age and higher serum lactate were independently associated with mortality. Conclusions: Repeat VA-ECMO cannulation was associated with meaningful survival after post-decannulation hemodynamic collapse. The observation that patients re-cannulated for ECPR had outcomes similar to, and numerically better than other major re-cannulation groups, challenges the assumption that repeat ECPR is uniformly futile and suggests that carefully selected patients may still derive substantial benefit. Younger age and less severe metabolic derangement at the time of re-cannulation were associated with improved outcomes.
nef4df25ee23f: Background: Significant heterogeneity exists in pediatric cardiac intensive care unit (CICU) populations that suffer in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA). While individual registries provide sizable cohorts, they lack diagnostic and procedural granularity. We propose a novel linkage of national cardiac arrest and pediatric cardiac critical care quality registries to evaluate IHCA in children with heart disease, characterize cardiac disease profiles, and identify unique outcome-related risk factors. Methods: We linked the American Heart Association’s Get With the Guidelines-Resuscitation (GWTG-R) and the Pediatric Cardiac Critical Care Consortium (PC 4 ) registries. We included medical (MC) and surgical (SC) cardiac patients < 18 years of age admitted to CICUs between 8/1/2014-2/13/2023 with an index IHCA event. Cross-referencing identified 22 centers participating in both registries (Fig. 1). Primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge (SHD). Secondary outcomes were return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), return of circulation via extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ROC), and survival with a favorable neurologic outcome (FNO) from GWTG-R, defined by pediatric cerebral performance category (PCPC) scores. A composite survival with FNO variable was created by adding neurologic complications collected in PC 4 to GWTG-R’s definition. Generalized linear mixed-effects models accounting for hospital clustering examined associations between illness categories, and within MC subgroups, with outcomes. Adjustment covariates included single ventricle (SV) and congenital heart disease (CHD) status derived from PC 4 . Results: A total of 1,012 children were evaluated (418 MC; 594 SC); 42% were infants, 27% were SV, 85% had CHD, and 51% of SC patients had STAT 4-5 operations (Table 1). IHCA cumulative incidence was 0.91% for STAT 1-3 and 4.6% for STAT 4-5. Median CPR duration was similar between groups (MC 9 [IQR 3-35] vs SC 13 [IQR 3-38] mins, p=0.10). Overall, SHD was 55%, FNO in survivors was 62%, and composite FNO in survivors was 53%. In multivariable models, MC patients had lower odds of SHD (OR 0.45 [0.32-0.62]), ROSC (OR 0.43 [0.27-0.69]) and ROC (OR 0.38 [0.24-0.58]) compared to SC groups (Table 2). Among MC cohorts, having CHD was associated with lower odds of ROSC (OR 0.35 [0.14-0.88]) and ROC (OR 0.44 [0.20-0.96]), but similar SHD versus those with structurally normal hearts. No differences in FNO or composite FNO were seen between MC and SC cohorts. Conclusion: In this linkage analysis, adjusted for covariates including SV and CHD status, MC patients had higher hospital mortality compared with SC patients. Although MC cohorts with CHD had lower rates of ROSC and ROC, SHD was similar to MC patients without CHD. This study framework enables new procedure- and complexity-specific insights not feasible in either registry alone to more accurately predict outcomes.
n93e4d23c4088: Background: In Japan, Emergency Medical Services (EMS) personnel must obtain prior approval from the hospital before transporting a patient, which can cause refusal of admission or delays in treatment. Pediatric patients may be particularly affected because hospitals and specialists capable of managing pediatric emergencies are limited. Although transport difficulty has been associated with adverse outcomes in adults, its impact in pediatric OHCA remains unclear. Hypothesis: Transport difficulty is associated with prolonged prehospital time and worse clinical outcomes in pediatric OHCA. Methods: We conducted a retrospective nationwide, population-based study using the All-Japan Utstein Registry linked with emergency transport records from 2021 to 2023. Pediatric patients (<20 years) with OHCA were included. Transport difficulty was defined as ≥4 hospital acceptance requests before transport. Total prehospital time (emergency call to hospital arrival) was categorized into call-to-scene arrival time, scene time (scene arrival to departure), and transport time (scene departure to hospital arrival). The primary outcome was 1-month survival. Secondary outcomes were a favorable neurological outcome (CPC 1-2) and prehospital ROSC. Primary analyses compared patients with transport difficulty (≥4 requests) and those without (≤3 requests). Exploratory analyses evaluated outcomes according to the number of hospital acceptance requests. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, initial rhythm, cause of arrest, population density, and regional pediatric healthcare resources, including pediatric intensive care units, pediatric core hospitals, and tertiary emergency centers. Results: Among 3,967 pediatric OHCA patients, transport difficulty occurred in 106 (2.7%) (Table 1). Patients with transport difficulty had no significant difference in call-to-scene arrival time compared to those without the difficulty (9 vs 9 min, p= 0.290) but had longer scene time (16 vs 10 min) and total prehospital time (47 vs 31 min) (both p<0.001) (Table 2). ROSC before hospital arrival (6.6% vs 8.3%, p=0.650), 1-month survival (6.6% vs 13.1%, p=0.070), and favorable neurological outcome (3.8% vs 4.8%, p=0.810) did not significantly differ between groups. In exploratory analyses, observed 1-month survival rates were 12.9% for 1 call (reference), 15.0% for 2 calls (adjusted OR 1.15 [95% CI 0.82-1.58]), 11.2% for 3 calls (adjusted OR 0.82 [95% CI 0.42-1.49]), and 6.6% for ≥4 calls (adjusted OR 0.57 [95% CI 0.23-1.23]) (Figure 1). Conclusions: Transport difficulty was associated with prolonged prehospital time in pediatric OHCA. Despite no statistically significant association, the adjusted odds ratio for survival decreased as the requests increased. Further analysis with a larger sample size is needed to clarify this association.
nd86f65f8da25: Background: Previous Japanese studies have reported worse outcomes after nighttime pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). However, detailed hour-by-hour temporal patterns and their relationship to arrest etiology remain unclear. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that pediatric OHCA outcomes would exhibit distinct temporal patterns beyond conventional nighttime and that these patterns would differ according to arrest etiology. Aims: To evaluate hour-by-hour associations between emergency call time and outcomes after pediatric OHCA in Japan. Methods: We conducted a retrospective nationwide observational study using the All-Japan Utstein Registry (2005-2023). Pediatric OHCA patients (<18 years) with known emergency call time were included. Cases with transport time >120 minutes were excluded. Multivariable logistic regression models evaluated hour-by-hour associations between emergency call time and 30-day outcomes using 12:00 PM as the reference hour. Models were adjusted for year, age, sex, witnessed arrest, dispatcher-assisted CPR instruction, bystander CPR, arrest etiology, and transport time. Subgroup analyses were performed according to arrest etiology and weekday/weekend status. Results: Among 31,386 pediatric OHCA patients, crude 30-day survival was 20.9% during daytime (09:00-16:59), 15.4% during transition periods (07:00-08:59 and 17:00-22:59), and 9.1% during nighttime (23:00-06:59). In hour-by-hour adjusted analyses relative to the 12:00 PM reference hour, adjusted odds of 30-day survival progressively declined overnight and during early morning hours, reaching the lowest value at 06:00 (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.30, 95% CI 0.24-0.38) (Figure). Similar temporal patterns were observed for favorable neurological survival, with the lowest adjusted odds also at 06:00 (aOR 0.29, 95% CI 0.21-0.40). An additional decline in both survival and favorable neurological outcomes was observed around 17:00. These temporal patterns were more pronounced in non-cardiac OHCA than cardiac OHCA. Patterns were similar between weekdays and weekends, and transport time did not meaningfully differ across hours of the day. Conclusion: Pediatric OHCA outcomes demonstrated distinct hour-by-hour temporal patterns not explained by transport time or weekday/weekend differences. These findings may reflect temporal vulnerabilities in pediatric arrest recognition, family supervision patterns, and operational transitions within emergency and hospital systems.
ne065acd4260c: Introduction: Though national resuscitation guidelines recommend against routine use of calcium except in special circumstances, it is often given during pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest (pIHCA) for its vasoactive qualities. While observational studies have consistently shown associations between intra-arrest calcium and increased mortality, these studies failed to account for the timing of calcium administration, leading to high risk for resuscitation time bias. Aim: To examine the association of early calcium with outcomes from pIHCA. Research Question: Is early calcium associated with decreased odds of survival to hospital discharge or ROSC? Methods: This was a single-center retrospective study including patients ≤18 years old who had a pulseless IHCA from 2013-2023. The exposure was early calcium, defined as calcium administration within 5 minutes of CPR initiation. To ensure a similar timeframe for early calcium exposure across the cohort, patients who received CPR for <5 minutes were excluded. The primary and secondary outcomes were survival to hospital discharge and sustained ROSC, respectively. Logistic treatment-effects estimation utilizing inverse-probability weighting via a propensity score was used. A regression model was used to balance the groups with covariates selected a priori based on a patient’s propensity to receive early calcium: age, initial rhythm, illness category, interventions in place before arrest, presence of hyperkalemia, and presence of hypocalcemia. Because illness category, initial rhythm, and hyperkalemia did not achieve balance after weighting, they were included as covariates in the outcome model. Results: Of 242 patients, 64 (26%) received early calcium. In the univariate analyses, patients who received early calcium were more likely to be younger, have cardiac malformations, baseline central nervous system depression, hepatic insufficiency, and vasoactive infusions in place prior to arrest (Table 1). Early calcium administration varied by event location and time of event (Table 2). The median duration of CPR was longer in the early calcium cohort (27 minutes) compared with no early calcium (19 minutes; p=0.038). For the primary and secondary analyses using weighted cohorts, there were no differences in survival to hospital discharge (aOR 0.97, 95%CI 0.5-1.87, p=0.9) or ROSC (aOR 0.54, 95%CI 0.28-1.04, p=0.065; Table 3). Conclusions: In this weighted pIHCA cohort, there were no statistically significant differences in odds of survival to discharge or ROSC between patients who did and did not receive calcium in the first 5 minutes of CPR. Further work is needed to understand various time points of calcium administration and its effect on outcomes.
n8d6625951da8: Introduction: Variation in outcomes after pediatric cardiac arrest may be driven by inconsistent adherence to Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) guidelines. Time to defibrillation is a key metric for patients with presenting rhythm of ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VF/pVT), and delays >2 minutes are associated with a lower likelihood of survival. Interventions to improve resuscitation performance, such as CPR coaching, may offload cognitive demands on resuscitation team leaders. Excess cognitive loading has been associated with diagnostic error due to cognitive biases. Pertinent biases include the framing bias, in which the way information is initially presented impacts clinical decision-making, and the anchoring bias, which creates overreliance on initial impressions. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that cognitive biases influence resuscitation performance in simulated pediatric cardiac arrest. Specifically, events framed as non-cardiac in origin (septic shock in an oncology patient) would result in simulation teams being slower to defibrillate shockable rhythms versus events framed with a cardiac etiology (myocarditis with ventricular dysfunction). Methods: This study is a secondary analysis of a simulation-based study conducted at a quaternary children’s hospital to evaluate the impact of room design on resuscitation practices. Simulation teams of physicians, NPs, RNs, and respiratory therapists participated in two simulations with different clinical prompts both leading to cardiac arrest with initial rhythm of pVT. Team-based performance variables were abstracted from audio and video recordings including time stamps for cardiac arrest, initiation of compressions, first dose of epinephrine (if given), and defibrillation. Chest compression quality data were collected via Zoll OneStep Electrodes. Results: For all 38 simulations, average time to defibrillation was 3.4 minutes (95% CI = 3.0-3.8 mins). In 47% of simulations, epinephrine was given before defibrillation, despite the presence of a shockable rhythm. For myocarditis scenarios, defibrillation was the first intervention 58% of the time, versus 47% of the time for septic shock, though the difference did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.51). In simulations where epinephrine was given first, time to defibrillation increased to 3.9 minutes (95% CI=3.1-4.7 min), versus 2.9 minutes (95% CI=2.6-3.3 min) for simulations where a shock was administered first (p = 0.011). Conclusions: Clinical framing in a simulated resuscitation may activate cognitive biases that impact adherence to PALS guidelines. Administering a dose of epinephrine as the first intervention resulted in a statistically significant delay in the time to appropriate defibrillation in simulated cardiac arrest with a presenting rhythm of pVT.
n0e4f4e1fa95f: Background: Adult and pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) have historically differed in baseline characteristics, etiologies, event features, interventions, and outcomes. Advances in arrest prevention and resuscitation practices may have narrowed these gaps, but contemporary comparisons are limited. We evaluated differences in characteristics and outcomes between pediatric and adult IHCA in a large national registry in North America. Methods: Using the GWTG-Resuscitation database, we identified index IHCA events requiring chest compressions for at least 1 minute between 2015 and 2024, excluding pandemic years 2020-2022. The exposure was age group (pediatric <18 years vs adult). Outcomes included survival to hospital discharge, return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), and favorable neurological outcome (adult cerebral performance category [CPC] 1–2 or pediatric CPC 1–3). Generalized estimating equations were used for clustering by hospital and event year; pre-arrest factors were treated as mediators. Standard mean differences (SMDs) with SMD >0.1 or <-0.1 indicated meaningful differences. Results: The cohort included 161,162 adults and 3,749 children with IHCA. Adults had lower odds of survival to discharge (26% vs 46%; odds ratio [OR] 0.44, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.41-0.47), favorable neurological outcome (18% vs 33%; OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.46-0.57), and ROSC (73% vs 78%; OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.74–0.88) compared with children. Adults were more likely to present with VF/pVT (16% vs 10%, SMD -0.17), yet lower adult survival persisted after stratifying by initial rhythm: for non-shockable rhythms, survival was 22% vs 44% (OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.48–0.52), and for shockable rhythms, 45% vs 52% (OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78–0.97) for adults and children respectively. Children were more likely than adults to arrest in an ICU (69% vs 38%; SMD 0.66), receive calcium during CPR (44% vs 35%; SMD 0.18), and undergo ECPR (12% vs <1%; SMD 0.50). Adults more commonly received sodium bicarbonate (55% vs 48%; SMD 0.15) and amiodarone (20% vs 5%; SMD 0.49) during CPR. Conclusion: In this large IHCA registry, adults had approximately half the odds of survival to discharge and favorable neurological outcome compared with children, despite only modestly lower odds of ROSC. These survival differences were not explained by initial rhythm and occurred in the setting of marked differences in care setting, pre-arrest support, and resuscitation practices, highlighting age-specific targets to improve outcomes. Future directions include contrasting etiology of arrest and post-arrest care practices.
n7e47247f962c: Introduction: Medical emergencies require rapid, coordinated responses to optimize outcomes; however, variability in training, role clarity, and adherence to evidence-based practices are common. To address these gaps, a multidisciplinary Resuscitation Committee was established to oversee clinical support, quality improvement, and education for a hospital’s Medical Emergency Response Team. With executive sponsorship, committee structure was designed to ensure accountability, frontline engagement, and system-level reliability. Research Questions: This initiative aimed to determine whether a structured, interdisciplinary resuscitation committee could improve guideline adherence, team preparedness, and patient outcomes. We hypothesized that a formalized committee model integrating practice, education, and quality review would enhance resuscitation performance and support sustained improvement in survival outcomes. Methods: The committee operates using a three-arm framework: Practice, Clinical Support, and Quality. The Practice arm standardizes workflows, equipment, and code processes, with continuous refinement based on real event feedback. The Clinical Support arm provides structured onboarding, simulation-based training, and annual competencies to reinforce role mastery and team dynamics. The Quality arm reviews all resuscitation events through weekly multidisciplinary debriefs and bi-monthly trend analysis, incorporating metrics such as ROSC, survival to discharge, neurologic outcomes, and adherence to AHA guidelines. Results: Committee membership grew from 10 members in 2019 to 49 in 2025, reflecting increased institutional engagement. Survival to discharge improved from 20.8% in 2017 to 29.3% in 2024, representing a 40% increase from baseline, with rates consistently above 28% in past years. The institution received the American Heart Association Get With The Guidelines-Gold Award from 2020-2025. Conclusion: A structured, interdisciplinary resuscitation committee using a three-arm model can drive measurable improvements in resuscitation performance, guideline adherence, and patient outcomes. Integrating frontline clinical staff into shared governance enables sustainable system-wide change, improved operational efficiency, and enhanced emergency response reliability. This model is scalable and replicable for organizations seeking to strengthen resuscitation systems and achieve high-level clinical performance recognition.
n1362bc0ae2d6: Introduction/Background: Successful management of in-hospital cardiac arrests (IHCAs) depends on timely interventions, effective communication, and coordinated teamwork. Healthcare organizations commonly monitor outcomes using measures such as spontaneous circulation, survival to discharge (STD), and resuscitation guideline adherence. Review of IHCAs at a Level One Academic Trauma Center revealed variability in responder numbers. Resuscitation event critiques suggested that excessive responders during IHCAs created barriers to communication, role clarity, and overall workflow efficiency. Quality improvement efforts primarily focus on clinical interventions and documentation accuracy, with less attention given to how physical environments may influence patient outcomes during IHCAs. Research Question/Hypothesis: Is there a relationship between responder overcrowding during an IHCA and survivability? Goals/Aims: The aim of this study was to evaluate the relationship between responder overcrowding during IHCA event survival and STD. Methods/Approach: This retrospective study reviewed resuscitation event critiques from 1/1/2023 to 12/31/25. Patients who underwent an IHCA were included and those under the age of 18 years, outpatients, visitors, experienced more than one IHCA, and emergency department and operating room events were excluded. The Chi-Square Test for Independence evaluated the potential association between the number of appropriate responders (i.e., ≤ 13 responders) versus overcrowded (i.e., ≥ 14 responders) and survival of an IHCA and STD (i.e., Expired or Survived). Yates’ Correction for Continuity was reported for both outcomes. Results/Data: A Chi-Square Test for Independence indicated no significant association between survivability of an IHCA event and crowd status, χ 2 (1, n = 290 = 0.610, p = 0.435, phi = -0.055. A Chi-Square Test for Independence indicated no significant association between STD and crowd status, χ 2 (1, n = 290 = 2.934, p = 0.087, phi = -0.111. Conclusions: Although there were no significant associations between survivability of an IHCA and crowd status, this project demonstrated clinical significance. For example, qualitatively exploring emergency team responder perceptions of crowd status and the impact on IHCAs. Future research implications include additional factors that may impact survivability such as deviations from Advanced Cardiac Life Support and post-cardiac arrest care guidelines.
n06a2367c8189: Background: Cardiac arrest affects over 500,000 Americans annually and remains a major public health challenge. Post-cardiac arrest shock—defined as inadequate oxygen delivery to vital organs—occurs in over 70% of initial survivors and contributes substantially to mortality and organ dysfunction. While post-arrest shock following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) has been extensively studied, data on in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) is limited. Research Objectives: The objectives of this study are to characterize the epidemiology, treatment patterns, and trajectory of shock following IHCA, including progression/resolution, evaluate associations with organ dysfunction, vasopressor selection, organ support, and clinical outcomes Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with IHCA using the Discover-IHCA registry. Post-arrest variables included vasoactive medication use, organ support methods, and cardiac sequential organ failure assessment score (cSOFA). The primary exposure was post-arrest shock; the primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge. Secondary outcomes included organ dysfunction requiring organ support, survival at 24, 48 and 72 hours. We present descriptive statistics as means or medians where appropriate. Paired comparisons between pre- and post-arrest organ support were performed using McNemars where appropriate. A covariate-adjusted logistic regression model was also developed. Results: We included 955 adult patients across 69 hospitals. Of these, 339 (35.5%) were female. The majority (42.2%) of individuals were age > 70 (Table 1). Primary respiratory causes were the most common etiology of arrest (n = 316, 33.1%), followed by primary cardiac (n = 250, 26.2%). A total of 742 patients (77.7%) experienced post-arrest shock, defined as any use of vasopressor/inotrope (n = 666, 69.7%), mechanical circulatory support (intra-aortic balloon pump/impella) (n = 30, 3.14%), or initiation of VA-ECMO (n = 46, 4.82%). Norepinephrine was the most common vasopressor (n = 709, 74.2%). Comparison of pre- versus post-arrest organ support showed significant increases in multiple interventions (Table 2). Higher weighted cSOFA burden was associated with higher odds of in-hospital death (OR =1.95, 95% CI 1.73-2.19, p < 0.001) (Figure 1). Conclusions: Over three-quarters of patients with IHCA suffer post-arrest shock. Significant increases in organ support occur after IHCA. Higher cSOFA scores post-arrest was strongly associated with in hospital death. Future analyses will explore patient centered outcomes and variations in IHCA management.
n36fa4c401344: Background: Cardiac arrest following endotracheal intubation is a rare but catastrophic complication in critically ill patients. Data describing its incidence, predictors, and outcomes in large ICU populations remain limited. We evaluated the incidence, risk factors, and outcomes of early post-intubation cardiac arrest (PICA) in a large critical care cohort. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the MIMIC-IV v3.1 database. Adult ICU patients undergoing endotracheal intubation were identified using procedure event records. The primary outcome was cardiac arrest occurring within 6 hours of the first recorded intubation. Secondary outcomes included cardiac arrest within 1 hour and 24 hours of intubation. Demographic characteristics, comorbidities, pre-intubation laboratory values, hemodynamic parameters, and vasopressor use were extracted. A prespecified multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify independent predictors of PICA. Results: A total of 8,463 intubated ICU stays were identified. Post-intubation cardiac arrest within 6 hours occurred in 62 patients (0.73%), including 40 arrests within 1 hour (0.47%) and 103 arrests within 24 hours (1.22%). Patients experiencing PICA had higher pre-intubation lactate levels (4.42±3.18 vs 2.98±2.70 mmol/L, p<0.001), higher heart rates (117.0±22.2 vs 104.9±23.5 beats/min, p<0.001), lower minimum systolic blood pressure (91.4±26.1 vs 105.9±25.4 mmHg, p<0.001), higher creatinine levels (2.22±1.77 vs 1.72±1.73 mg/dL, p=0.030), and higher white blood cell counts (16.7±10.5 vs 13.7±10.4 х10 9 /L, p=0.032). Heart failure (43.5% vs 30.3%, p=0.033), sepsis (53.2% vs 31.6%, p<0.001), shock (17.7% vs 6.7%, p=0.001), and pre-intubation vasopressor use (33.9% vs 22.0%, p=0.036) were more common among patients who developed PICA.Hospital mortality was substantially higher among patients with PICA compared with those without PICA (82.3% vs 28.1%, p<0.001). In multivariable analysis, higher pre-intubation heart rate (adjusted OR 1.161 per 10 beats/min, 95% CI 1.020-1.306) and lower pre-intubation mean arterial pressure (adjusted OR 0.698 per 10 mmHg, 95% CI 0.560-0.869) were independently associated with PICA. Elevated lactate (adjusted OR 1.09 per mmol/L, 95% CI 0.99-1.17) and creatinine (adjusted OR 1.12 per mg/dL, 95% CI 0.98-1.24) demonstrated modest associations that did not reach statistical significance. Conclusions: Post-intubation cardiac arrest occurred in approximately 1 in 137 intubated ICU patients and was associated with extremely high in-hospital mortality exceeding 80%. Pre-intubation tachycardia and hypotension independently identified patients at the highest risk, suggesting the hypothesis that hemodynamic optimization before intubation may be an important target for prevention.
n71baebc53ab9: Background: ECG rhythm assessment during resuscitation of ventricular fibrillation/tachycardia (VF/VT) out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) requires CPR interruption because CPR causes ECG artifacts. Ideally defibrillators would use artificial intelligence (AI) for binary (non-shockable vs. shockable) and 3-class (asystole [ASY] vs. organized [ORG] vs. shockable [VF/VT]) ECG classification during CPR to guide diagnosis and treatment. However, algorithm development is challenged by a paucity of OHCA ECGs, particularly during CPR. Goal: We built generative AI models to synthesize OHCA ECGs with and without CPR artifact to (1) determine whether classifiers trained with synthetic (artificial) ECGs can classify real (clinical) ECGs, and (2) compare performance between classifiers trained with real vs. synthetic ECGs. Methods: We performed a retrospective study of adult VF-OHCA from 2006-2021 in a metropolitan EMS system. Patients were randomized 80%/20% for training/test. Defibrillator pad ECGs clipped into 2.5-s segments were manually labeled by CPR and rhythm (ASY, ORG, VF, VT) by expert reviewers. Using training ECGs, we first developed generative adversarial networks (GAN) and diffusion models (DM) to synthesize ASY, ORG, and VF/VT ECGs with and without CPR. Then using (1) the real training ECGs, (2) GAN-generated ECGs, and (3) DM-generated ECGs, classifiers were trained for binary (ASY/ORG vs. VF/VT) and 3-class (ASY vs. ORG vs. VF/VT) rhythm prediction. Classifiers included 1-D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with ECG voltages as inputs and 2-D CNNs with ECG scalograms as inputs. To evaluate synthetic data utility, we compared classifiers trained with real vs. synthetic data in the test dataset using binary (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC], F1 score) and 3-class (balanced accuracy [BAC]) metrics. Results: The cohort had 2011 patients with 1.03 million ECGs (60% with CPR). Classifiers were trained on real, GAN-generated, and DM-generated datasets of 816134 ECGs each (Figure). In the test dataset of 213664 ECGs from 402 patients, classifiers trained with synthetic data had good binary performance without CPR (AUC=0.97-0.99, F1=0.78-0.87) and with CPR (AUC=0.95-0.96, F1=0.84-0.86) (Table 1), and moderate 3-class performance without CPR (BAC=65-85%) and with CPR (BAC=62-84%) (Table 2). On average, classifiers trained with real data outperformed those trained with synthetic data by an AUC of 0.019 (vs. GAN) and 0.016 (vs. DM), F1 of 0.084 (vs. GAN) and 0.081 (vs. DM), and BAC of 4.4% (vs. GAN) and 6.1% (vs. DM). Conclusions: Generative models successfully synthesized ECGs with and without CPR. Classifiers trained on synthetic data had slightly reduced performance versus those trained on real data. The results suggest potential for on-demand synthesis of OHCA ECGs, enabling AI sandboxing and development of next-generation ECG algorithms.
n62df668fe8b8: Background: During ventricular fibrillation (VF), conventional ECG interpretation cannot identify acute coronary occlusion (ACO). Rapid detection of ACO during out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) could facilitate targeted resuscitation and triage strategies. Hypothesis: Artificial intelligence (AI) analysis of VF waveforms can distinguish ischemic VF caused by ACO from non-ischemic VF without coronary occlusion. Methods: Female Yorkshire swine undergoing standardized VF OHCA experiments were classified as ischemic VF (I-VF) following proximal left anterior descending artery occlusion or non-ischemic VF (N-VF) induced without coronary occlusion. Lead II ECGs sampled at 250 Hz during the first 3 minutes of untreated VF were segmented into 10-second windows. Four AI models were developed: convolutional neural network (CNN), random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM), and decision tree (DT). Model development used 4-fold cross-validation on 56 animals (20 I-VF, 36 N-VF) with oversampling of the minority class to address class imbalance. An independent, balanced holdout test set of 16 animals (8 I-VF, 8 N-VF) assessed generalizability. Performance was evaluated using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals (CI), and DeLong testing. Results: The CNN demonstrated superior discrimination compared with all other models in both the development and test datasets (all p<0.05 by DeLong testing). In the development dataset, the CNN achieved an AUC of 0.93 (95% CI 0.91-0.94), sensitivity of 0.84 (95% CI 0.79-0.87), and specificity of 0.89 (95% CI 0.86-0.91). Performance remained robust in the independent test dataset, with an AUC of 0.91 (95% CI 0.88-0.94), sensitivity of 0.85 (95% CI 0.79-0.90), and specificity of 0.83 (95% CI 0.77-0.89). At a clinically relevant fixed sensitivity of 90%, specificity was 0.76 (95% CI 0.66-0.86) on the test set. Conclusions: AI-based analysis of VF waveforms can identify ACO during active VF with clinically meaningful accuracy in a porcine model of OHCA. If validated in human cohorts, this approach could support real-time triage, reperfusion decision-making, and personalized resuscitation strategies during VF cardiac arrest.
nd2e465681d50: Introduction: Video review is a powerful resource in quality improvement and research of high mortality rates of out-of-hospital cardiac arrests (OHCAs). Manual review is time and resource-intensive, limiting implementation at scale. Hypothesis: Automating the video review process is feasible using Artificial Intelligence (AI). Aim: We assessed the feasibility and accuracy of Google’s Gemini AI in reviewing cardiac arrest resuscitation simulations in the Emergency Department (ED). Methods: Eight pediatric OHCA simulation videos with identical scenarios were reviewed by trained investigators and Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro model. Data points were extracted blinded to study results. Inter-rater reliability of reviewers was 0.78. Simulations included a team leader, charting nurse, medication nurse, and four research actors (CPR provider/coach, bedside nurse, airway provider). Videos were captured with a GoPro Hero 12 Black camera and compressed using HandBrake to optimize AI processing. AI was instructed to act as a clinical expert in cardiac resuscitation, tasked with reviewing technical and non-technical aspects of care. Human reviewers and AI were given definitions of each critical event, Concise Assessment of Leader Management (CALM) tool, and teamwork assessment (TEAM) tool. Technical variables included critical event timestamps (cardiac arrest recognition, compression initiation, pulse/rhythm assessment/identification). Non-technical variables included TEAM and CALM scores. Human vs AI results were compared using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) values and Bland Altman plots. Results: AI demonstrated excellent agreement with humans on technical variables (ICC ≥0.94). A total of 142 timestamps were included, with 9 events (6.3%) discordant between human and AI. Time to critical events showed a mean difference of -2.32 seconds with limits of agreement from -12.76 to +8.12 seconds (Figure 1), reflecting expected variability across clinical actions. Non-technical variable agreement was moderate. TEAM scores showed a mean difference of 7.25 points (range 1.83 to 12.67) (Figure 2); CALM scores showed a mean difference of 1.12 points (range -7.15 to 9.40) (Figure 3). ICC for non-technical variables were poor (TEAM: 0.022, CALM: 0.31). Conclusions: AI showed excellent concordance for technical metrics but requires refinement for non-technical variables. Results support automating video analysis of cardiac resuscitation to improve efficiency and scalability.
n7b8becd5b6f9: Introduction: The cause of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) often remains unknown because most patients die before comprehensive diagnostic evaluation can be performed. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that healthcare data can be leveraged to infer plausible causes that are not captured by conventional investigations. Aims: The aims of our study was to develop and assess a “numerical autopsy” framework that infer probabilistic etiologic profiles for unexplained OHCA using longitudinal healthcare data. Methods: We conducted a retrospective population based study linking the Paris Cardiac Arrest Center registry with the French National Health Insurance database. Adults with non-traumatic OHCA occurring between May 2011 and May 2020 were included. Five-year pre-arrest hospital diagnoses, outpatient drug dispensations, procedures, and registry variables were aggregated into 393 standardized features. A calibrated multiclass Light Gradient Boosting Machine model was trained on clinically adjudicated cases to predict six etiologic categories: cardiac ischemic, cardiac other, hypoxic, embolic, neurologic, and other. Cases with initially unknown etiology were reclassified only when the highest predicted probability was ≥ 50%. Results: Among 22,170 eligible patients, 3,353 had an adjudicated etiology and 18,817 remained unexplained after standard evaluation. On a held-out random test set, the model achieved a log-loss of 1.07, an overall one-vs-rest AUROC of 0.79, a F1-score of 0.37, and 63% accuracy. Temporal validation showed similar performance, with log-loss of 1.04, AUROC of 0.81, and macro F1-score of 0.36. After numerical autopsy, the proportion of unknown etiologies decreased from 84.9% to 53.1%. Ischemic etiologies increased from 7.5% to 20.2%, and hypoxic etiologies from 3.0% to 21.4%. Explainability analyses showed clinically coherent patterns, including respiratory variables among hypoxic reclassifications and cardiovascular variables among cardiac reclassifications. Conclusions: Numerical autopsy provides a scalable, uncertainty-aware approach to reclassifying unexplained OHCA using routine longitudinal healthcare data. It does not replace clinical adjudication or post-mortem investigation but may support etiologic surveillance and prevention-oriented review when conventional diagnostic information is incomplete.
nd657ddb3fda5: Anoxic brain injury (ABI) classification after cardiac arrest is critical to determining eligibility for neuroprotective therapies such as therapeutic hypothermia. Subjectivity in determining injury severity on diagnostics such as CT confound and delay accurate classification and prognostication. The current standard for objective CT-based ABI classification relies on manual gray-white matter ratio (GWR) measurement, which is time-intensive and limited by variability across CT scanners, hindering its utility for time-sensitive decision-making in the early post-arrest window. In this study, we introduce contrastive language and image reasoning with masked autoencoders (CLAIR), a novel multimodal framework integrating head computed tomography (CT) imaging with non-imaging clinical patient information through a cross-attention mechanism and contrastive learning approach to predict dichotomized cerebral performance category (CPC) score in patients after cardiac arrest. We benchmarked CLAIR against manual measurements and an automated, CT only-based masked autoencoder approach (CT-MAE) in a retrospective study of 208 patients with CT scans obtained within the first 24 hours of arrest. Manual GWR and CT-MAE achieved comparable overall discriminative performance (AUC-ROC: 0.87 and 0.80, respectively); however, manual GWR was limited by low specificity (0.54), with important implications for withdrawal-of-care decisions, while CT-MAE offered the advantage of full automation without sacrificing accuracy. Critically, neither imaging-only approach alone achieved sufficient predictive performance to independently guide clinical decision-making. In contrast, CLAIR achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.94 (CI: 0.90-0.97) when trained on multiplanar CT reconstructions combined with non-imaging clinical data, significantly outperforming CT-based imaging-only methods (p = 0.03) and surpassing the manual GWR clinical standard. To further evaluate clinical utility of CLAIR, we conducted a structured clinical assessment comparing CLAIR against two clinicians, a senior neurology resident and an attending neurointensivist, across a series of tests simulating varying levels of information availability during the post-arrest course. Clinicians assisted by CLAIR predictions made fewer prognostic errors than in their non-assisted assessments. Our results suggest that CLAIR can contribute value as a clinical assistive tool aiming at reliable ABI classification for post-cardiac arrest patients, potentially enabling more timely clinical decision-making, family counseling, and resource allocation.
n7a6ac90410d7: Background: Refractory ventricular fibrillation (R-VF) out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients—pragmatically defined as those requiring ≥3 shocks—experience lower likelihood of resuscitation and survival compared to non-refractory patients. R-VF subtypes can further stratify patients by prognosis which could help guide treatment. Specifically, incessant R-VF (shocks fail to terminate VF) fare worse than recurrent R-VF (shocks terminate VF but VF recurs); hence incessant R-VF outcomes may be improved with targeted, alternative treatment strategies. However, identification of incessant R-VF has been limited to retrospective studies requiring post-hoc ECG rhythm review, challenging real-time implementation of a targeted strategy. We evaluated whether a deep learning-based rhythm classification algorithm designed for real-time use can determine shock response to classify patients by R-VF subtype as a means to consider clinical implementation of subtype-specific therapies. Objective: We evaluated automated classification of individual VF shock responses and patient-level R-VF subtypes using a “see-through-CPR” rhythm identification algorithm. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of adult VF-OHCA from 2006-21 from a metropolitan EMS system using continuous defibrillator ECG recordings. The gold standard annotation used a previously-published, 2-person review of immediate post-shock rhythm to determine shock-specific response (incessant vs. recurrent) and consequent patient-level classification (incessant only, recurrent only, or mixed). These annotations were compared with predictions from a previously-described deep learning rhythm classifier. Data were split into training and test sets. We selected a VF probability cut point that maximized F1 score in the training set for classifying shock-specific R-VF subtypes, and calculated accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of the automated algorithm relative to the gold standard annotations. Results: Among 1790 VF patients, median age was 62, 392 (22%) were female, 999 (56%) were refractory, and 760 (43%) survived with favorable status. Based on the gold standard annotations, R-VF shock-specific response was incessant in 35% and recurrent in 65% of shocks, producing patient-level classification of 16% incessant only, 46% recurrent only, and 37% mixed. Among the R-VF test set, the algorithm achieved a shock-specific accuracy of 93% (Table 1) and a patient-level 3-category accuracy of 88% (Table 2), with an incessant classification sensitivity of 0.81 (43/53) and specificity of 0.98 (276/282). Conclusions: An automated “see-through-CPR” rhythm identification algorithm can evaluate shock-specific rhythm response to achieve classification of R-VF subtypes including incessant R-VF, providing the potential to guide differential treatment strategies in real-time.
n33f46a822bb0: Introduction: Recurrent cardiac arrest (rearrest) affects up to half of patients who achieve return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) and is associated with worse outcomes. Predicting rearrest may enable preemptive EMS interventions. Evidence to date indicates clinical ECG features provide modest, time-dependent prediction of rearrest, performing better as rearrest approaches, potentially too late for intervention. Machine learning-based feature extraction may capture ECG signatures not detected by clinical measures. Goal: We evaluated a data-driven approach for rearrest prediction using ECG waveform data. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of adult OHCA patients treated by urban Emergency Medical Services (EMS) between 2018 and 2024 who achieved ROSC. We developed and evaluated a machine learning model to predict rearrest using a 5-minute ECG segment spanning the 6 to 1 minute period before rearrest. Patients were randomized 80/20% into training and test sets. ECGs were divided into 15-second segments and transformed into scalograms ( Figure 1 ). Principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to the training data, and the top 20 principal components (measured by variance captured) were used as inputs to an XGBoost classifier. Hyperparameters were optimized using a grid search with 10-fold cross-validation. To provide a comparative baseline versus the data-driven model, a clinical model was also developed using heart rate, heart rate variability, and QRS duration as inputs for logistic regression. Performance was evaluated by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Results: Of the 1,247 OHCA patients who achieved ROSC, 526 (42%) experienced rearrest. The AUROC of the data driven model and the clinical model were 0.48-0.65 and 0.49-0.74, respectively. The data-driven model demonstrated relatively stable predictive performance across the entire evaluated pre-rearrest ( Figure 2 ). In contrast, the clinical model showed greater temporal dependence, with AUROC values improving as rearrest approached. At earlier timepoints, the data-driven approach’s AUROC point estimates exceeded the clinical model’s, whereas the clinical model AUROC point estimates were higher closer to rearrest. Conclusion: Rearrest prediction did not differ between machine learning versus clinical ECG measures, though these models differed with regard to time-dependent prediction. Machine learning-based feature extraction may complement conventional ECG models to predict impending rearrest, enabling earlier and more robust identification of patients at risk.
n2ed341140a0e: Background: Hemorrhagic shock and resuscitation cause ischemia-reperfusion injury, endothelial glycocalyx degradation, vascular dysfunction, and organ injury. Although transfusion is essential, strategies that improve resuscitation efficiency and reduce blood product requirements are needed. The effect of hydrogen gas (H 2 ), which has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, during transfusion-based resuscitation remains unknown. Hypothesis: H 2 inhalation would reduce transfusion requirements without compromising hemodynamic or metabolic recovery and would attenuate endothelial and organ injury. Methods: Twenty male Sprague-Dawley rats underwent pressure-controlled hemorrhagic shock. Blood was withdrawn to maintain mean arterial pressure at 30-35 mmHg for 60 minutes, followed by shed-blood transfusion over 60 minutes to achieve predefined hemodynamic targets. Animals were randomized to control gas or 1.3% H 2 gas inhalation, which was initiated 15 minutes before resuscitation and continued throughout resuscitation. Hemodynamics, arterial blood gas variables, lactate, transfusion volume, and plasma syndecan-1 were evaluated during the acute resuscitation phase. Animals were followed for 24 hours, after which blinded histopathological scoring of kidney, small-intestinal, and liver injury was performed. Results: Shed blood volume was similar between the H 2 and control groups (10.8 vs 10.4 mL; P=0.64), whereas transfused blood volume was significantly lower with H 2 (4.7 vs 6.9 mL; P<0.02). Despite receiving less transfusion, H 2 -treated rats maintained post-resuscitation hemodynamics and arterial blood gas parameters comparable to controls throughout the acute observation period, indicating that reduced transfusion did not compromise circulatory stabilization. Lactate did not increase after resuscitation in the H 2 group, and lactate normalization occurred more frequently with H 2 than with control gas (67% vs 38%; P=0.23). Plasma syndecan-1 after resuscitation was lower with H 2 , consistent with attenuated endothelial glycocalyx shedding (900 vs 1140 pg/mL; P<0.01). H 2 also reduced renal tubular injury (Paller score, 4 vs 9; P<0.01) and intestinal mucosal injury (Chiu-Park score, 0.5 vs 4; P<0.01). Liver injury scores were lower with H 2 , although the difference was not statistically significant (2.0 vs 6.5; P=0.24). Conclusions: H 2 inhalation improved transfusion-based resuscitation efficiency by reducing transfusion requirements while preserving hemodynamic stability and lactate clearance. Attenuation of endothelial glycocalyx shedding and kidney and intestinal injury suggests that H 2 may be a promising, resource-sparing adjunct for hemorrhagic shock resuscitation.
n2ebc60837783: Introduction: Brain injury is a major contributor to post-cardiac arrest (CA) morbidity and mortality, yet the synaptic and molecular mechanisms governing these outcomes remain poorly understood. We have previously shown that Dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1), a regulator of mitochondrial fission, is activated in the heart immediately following resuscitation and is an important determinant of myocardial function. Drp1 is also critical for maintaining normal synaptic function, but its relationship to post-CA neurophysiology is unknown. Here, we evaluated acute post-CA changes in synaptic physiology and Drp1 expression at the CA3-CA1 synapse of the hippocampus, a region with well-characterized ischemic vulnerability and a central role in activity-dependent plasticity, at 3 and 7 hours (h) post-CA. Methods: In an established murine model of CA, we characterized the neurophysiology of the CA3-CA1 synapse using field electrophysiological recordings, at 3h and 7h post-CA to characterize the input-output relationship, paired-pulse facilitation (PPF) and short-term and long-term potentiation (PPF). We also evaluated changes in total Drp1 and Drp1 phosphorylation, and total CaMKII and CaMKII T286 phosphorylation, in the hippocampus and in the heart, at 3h and 7h post-CA. Results: In the hippocampus, we observed impairment in baseline transmission as seen in the input-output curve at the CA1-CA3 synapse (p<0.05) as well as in synaptic functions, such as short-term potentiation (p<0.01) and long-term potentiation, LTP (p<0.0001) at both 3h and 7h post-CA, congruent with loss of postsynaptic function. Additionally, paired-pulse facilitation (PPF) was only impaired at 7h post-CA (p<0.05), indicating the generalization of injury to presynaptic sites. We also measured total Drp1 and Drp1 phosphorylation at these timepoints, and our results demonstrate that inactivating Drp1-S637 phosphorylation is downregulated in the heart (p<0.05) at 3h and 7h post-ROSC. However, in the hippocampus, activating Drp1-S616 phosphorylation is upregulated only at 7h (p<0.01), indicating increase in mitochondrial fission markers at 3h and 7h in the heart but only at 7h in the brain. We also evaluated total CaMKII protein and CaMKII T286 phosphorylation in the hippocampus at both timepoints, and saw a decrease in total CaMKII protein (p<0.05) at 3h and 7h post-ROSC. Conclusion: Post-CA injury in the hippocampus is dynamic and progressive in the hours following resuscitation, in contrast to the more acutely injured heart. These findings demonstrate that the brain and heart follow unique post-CA timelines, suggestive of distinct windows of organ specific opportunity for therapeutic intervention.
neb326d7b1c41: Background: Traditional cardiac arrest resuscitation relies heavily on high-dose epinephrine to achieve return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and on continued vasopressors to support hemodynamics after ROSC. Despite high doses of vasopressors, many patients continue to re-arrest after ROSC and have substantial cerebral ischemia. We evaluated whether automated, titratable endovascular partial aortic occlusion to offset epinephrine requirements could mitigate secondary injury, eliminate post-ROSC rearrest, and preserve cerebral perfusion compared to standard vasopressor-based management. Methods: Ventricular fibrillation was induced in 20 anesthetized Yorkshire swine. Following a 5-minute no-flow injury phase, mechanical CPR and automated Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS)-guided resuscitation were initiated. Animals achieving ROSC were randomized to automated critical care for 12 hours (Control, n=10) or endovascular perfusion augmentation for critical care (EPACC, n=6) for 6 hours, followed by an additional 6 hours of automated critical care. Automated critical care used MAP, CVP, fluid responsiveness, lactate, and urine output as input variables for determining the need for weight-based crystalloid boluses and titration of epinephrine and vasopressin. Automated aortic balloon-augmentation created a goal blood pressure gradient of 10 mmHg across the balloon within Zone 1 of the descending thoracic aorta. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed on all surviving animals at 12 hours after ROSC. Results: A total of 12 animals survived to MRI evaluation (EPACC, n=6; Control, n=6); 4 control animals expired early due to re-arrest. Automated balloon support achieved a 100% survival rate and eliminated rearrests, compared with 40% early mortality and a significant rearrest rate in the control group (p = 0.03). While macro-hemodynamics (mean arterial pressure, carotid blood flow) and total epinephrine and fluid requirements were comparable between groups, laser Doppler flowmetry demonstrated significantly higher cerebral microvascular perfusion in the EPACC group during the first hour after balloon deflation (p < 0.05). MRI revealed smaller cerebral infarct volumes and superior sum ASPECTS in the EPACC group compared to Controls (Figure 1, p < 0.05). EPACC animals exhibited a minor, non-significant increase in peak creatinine. Conclusions: Automated, dynamic endovascular aortic occlusion successfully bridged the post-ROSC "hemodynamic cliff," preventing rearrest and significantly reducing cerebral infarction. These data demonstrate that second-to-second automated titration of afterload provides neuroprotection and preserves micro-perfusion during the early post-ROSC phase.
nf4b0eb82ebcc: Introduction: The potential impact of Resuscitative Endovascular Balloon Occlusion of the Aorta (REBOA) during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) remains controversial. Little is known about the potential survival benefit of REBOA combined with head-up cardiopulmonary resuscitation (AHUP-CPR). Research question: The primary study objective was to compare the 24-hour survival after conventional (C) CPR+REBOA, AHUP-CPR alone, or AHUP-CPR+REBOA. Additional survival and hemodynamic outcomes were assessed. Methods: This was an experimental, prospective, controlled, randomized study. After isoflurane anesthesia, preparation and induction of ventricular fibrillation (VF), Yorkshire pigs were randomized in three groups: C-CPR+REBOA, AHUP alone and AHUP+REBOA. After 10 minutes of untreated VF, 18 minutes of C-CPR or AHUP-CPR (combination of an impedance threshold device, active compression-decompression and progressive head and thorax elevation) was provided. REBOA was inflated after 15 min (Figure 1) of CPR. Using Kaplan-Meier and a log-rank tests, 24-hour survival was compared between groups. Return of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC), and favorable neurologic function at 24 hours (FN-24, defined as a Cerebral Performance Category score of 1 or 2) were assessed. Decompression aortic blood pressure (DBP), coronary perfusion pressure (CorPP), end-tidal CO2 (EtCO 2 ) and cerebral oximetry (rSO 2 ) before (14min) and after (17min) REBOA inflation were measured. Results: With 10 pigs per group, ROSC rates were 20% with C-CPR+REBOA, 60% with AHUP alone, and 90% with AHUP+REBOA (p = 0.008), respectively. Differences in 24h survival were also significantly different between groups (0% C-CPR+REBOA, 30% AHUP alone, and 30% AHUP+REBOA; log-rank p = 0.008; Fig. 2). Median (Q1; Q3) survival times were 0 h (0; 0) with C-CPR+REBOA, 4.25 h (0.0; 19.5) with AHUP alone, and 7.5 h (6.0; 20.0) with AHUP+REBOA (p = 0.002). FN-24 was 0% with C-CPR+REBOA, 30% with AHUP alone and 30% with AHUP+REBOA (p = 0.15).Detailed hemodynamic data are presented in Table 1. Before REBOA inflation (14 min of CPR), EtCO2 differed significantly among the three groups (p < 0.001). After REBOA inflation (17 min of CPR), DBP, CorPP, and EtCO2 differed significantly among the three groups (p = 0.04, p = 0.03, and p < 0.001, respectively). Conclusion: In this preclinical study, AHUP-CPR alone or with REBOA, significantly increased 24-hour survival rate and hemodynamics compared with C-CPR+REBOA.
nd30e8d30e1c3: Background: Oxygen administration following cardiac arrest (CA) is associated with cardiac dysfunction, brain injury, and poor survival. These injuries are driven in part by mitochondrial injury, but the metabolic consequences of post-CA hyperoxia remain incompletely understood. We hypothesized that post-CA hyperoxia produces histotoxic dysoxia — impaired cellular oxygen utilization despite adequate arterial oxygenation. Methods: In a murine model of CA, mice underwent 12 minutes of asystole followed by CPR. Beginning 30 minutes post-resuscitation, mice were exposed to 30% O 2 for 6 hours. Systemic metabolic parameters, including core body temperature, whole-body oxygen consumption (V̇O 2 ), and arterial blood gas values (pH, PO 2 , SaO 2 ) were assessed. Results: Post-CA exposure to 30% O 2 induced a systemic metabolic crisis characterized by hypothermia (35.0±0.3 vs. 37.3±0.1°C, p<0.005, n=3-4) and markedly suppressed V̇O 2 (2.1±1.0 vs. 9.1±1.3 mL/kg/min, p<0.001, n=5) compared to sham animals receiving identical oxygen treatment. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated severe acidosis (pH 6.91±0.03 vs. 7.19±0.01, p<0.001, n=8-10). Notably, arterial PO 2 and SaO 2 were preserved and did not differ from sham (p>0.05, n=8-10), indicating that metabolic injury occurred independently of arterial hypoxemia. Conclusions: Post-CA hyperoxia produced systemic hypothermia, suppressed whole-body oxygen consumption, and severe acidosis. Despite normal arterial PO 2 and SaO 2 , these findings indicate a failure of cellular oxygen utilization rather than delivery. This pattern is consistent with histotoxic dysoxia and implicates mitochondrial dysfunction as a central mechanism of post-resuscitation metabolic injury.
n4c03d7993bf4: Objective: Post-cardiac arrest syndrome (PCAS) is characterized by a rapid, dysregulated inflammatory response that exacerbates organ injury and undermines recovery. Extracellular vesicle-encapsulated mitochondrial DNA has recently been identified as a potent stimulus of post-resuscitation immune cell activation via the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway. Whether pharmacological cGAS inhibition can attenuate the post-resuscitation inflammatory response in vivo is unknown. Accordingly, we tested the hypothesis that cGAS inhibition attenuates the early post-resuscitation transcriptomic inflammatory response in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) after cardiac arrest. Methods: Swine (n=14) underwent 7 minutes of ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest and subsequent resuscitation. After return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), animals were randomized to receive a small molecule inhibitor of cGAS (G140; 0.1 mg/kg IV; n=7) or vehicle (n=7) at 15 minutes post-ROSC. PBMCs were isolated at baseline and 4 hours post-ROSC for bulk RNA sequencing. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using DESeq2 (adjusted p<0.05). Results: PBMCs from vehicle-treated animals exhibited 3,145 DEGs at 4 hours post-ROSC compared with baseline, reflecting widespread transcriptomic activation. G140-treated animals exhibited only 719 DEGs (77% reduction vs. vehicle; Figure, A ). Expression of cGAS itself was unchanged, consistent with pharmacological inhibition of enzymatic activity rather than gene expression. However, TBK1, the kinase immediately downstream of STING that phosphorylates IRF3, was significantly downregulated in G140-treated animals (log 2 FC=–0.39, p_adj=0.04). Additional genes within the cGAS-STING and innate immune signaling pathways were suppressed in G140- vs. vehicle-treated animals, including NLRP3, IL-15, TNFRSF11A, CCL14, and CCL21 ( Figure, B ). Conclusion: Systemic cGAS inhibition with G140 administered shortly after ROSC markedly attenuates the early post-resuscitation transcriptomic inflammatory response in porcine PBMCs. These findings support cGAS-STING as a tractable therapeutic target and provide rationale for further evaluation of cGAS inhibition as a targeted immunomodulatory strategy in PCAS.
n5dd5507f32f1: Introduction: The role of pyroptosis, a highly inflammatory form of programmed cell death, in cardiac injury following cardiac arrest is unknown. Related to pyroptosis, our prior work has shown that both oxidant injury and intracellular NAD levels result in significant cardiac injury and protection respectively. A better understanding of how oxidant stress and NAD metabolism affect cardiomyocyte injury and pyroptosis could identify new targets for cardiac arrest care. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that cardiac oxidant exposure induces NAD depletion and pyroptosis, which can be rescued by replenishment of cellular NAD. Methods: H9C2 cardiomyocytes were exposed to H 2 O 2 to create oxidative stress. Cell morphological change was observed under microscope, and cell viability was measured by CCK8 kit based on intracellular LDH activity. The expressions of GSDMD and GSDME and their N-terminal fragments were assessed by Western blot analysis. Intracellular NAD content was measured by assay kit. Results: H 2 O 2 induced a dose-dependent death of H9C2 cardiomyocytes, which plateaued at 1 mM and this death was related to NAD + depletion. H9C2 cells exhibited characteristic morphological changes of pyroptosis, such as cell swelling and rupture of the cell membrane, and release of LDH. Supplement with 1 mM NAM, a NAD + precursor, partially rescued viability in H 2 O 2 -treated cells from 54.9 ±1.7% to 81.7 ± 2.2% at 4h (p<0.01). The Nampt inhibitor FK866 (1 μM), which blocks NAD synthesis, totally nullified the protective effect of NAM on cell viability. The pan-caspase inhibitor Z-vad (100 μM) blocked the typical morphology of pyroptosis induced by H 2 O 2 . NAM also restored NAD + concentrations. To determine which gasdermin is involved in oxidant-induced cell death, cardiomyocytes were treated with 1 mM H 2 O 2 for up to 5 hrs. Both GSDME and its Asp270 cleavage N-terminal fragment were observed, and GSDME-N expression peaked after 2h exposure to H 2 O 2 . It was blocked by treatment with NAM or a caspase 3 inhibitor, but not by the NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950. Although GSDMD was cleaved after 2h exposure, there was no expression of the cleaved GSDMD (Asp275) N-terminal fragment. Conclusion: Cardiac oxidant injury, known to occur during cardiac arrest, can result in pyroptotic cell death that is mediated by caspases and can be rescued by NAD precursor treatment.
n718c839d5a68: Introduction: In austere settings, prolonged bag-valve-mask (BVM) ventilation may be required before advanced airway support is available. Excessive inspiratory flow, elevated airway pressures, and inconsistent tidal volumes during sustained manual ventilation increase the risk of lung injury and provider fatigue. Sotair is a flow-modulating accessory designed to improve ventilation safety during prolonged manual ventilation. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that Sotair would improve ventilation safety by limiting excessive inspiratory flow, airway pressure, and tidal volume delivery while maintaining physiologic stability compared to ventilation with a sham device. Methods: Twenty-two juvenile domestic swine (mean weight 52 ± 4 kg) were enrolled and assigned to 6-hour (n=8) or 24-hour (n=14) ventilation cohorts in a non-survival model of prolonged manual overventilation. Animals underwent intubation, invasive hemodynamic monitoring, hourly arterial blood gas sampling, and prolonged manual ventilation with a BVM system using either an active Sotair or sham device. Respiratory rate was titrated to end-tidal CO 2, and sham ventilation was delivered with forceful manual respirations to model excessive ventilation conditions. Airway flow, peak airway pressure, and tidal volume were continuously recorded, and gross lung injury was assessed at necropsy. Longitudinal physiologic data were analyzed using generalized estimating equations and mixed-effects regression models. Results: Twenty-one animals were analyzed after protocol violation: 8 in the 6-hour cohort (4 sham, 4 Sotair) and 13 in the 24-hour cohort (7 sham, 6 Sotair). Across 124,350 breaths over 360 observation hours, Sotair significantly reduced average inspiratory flow (–46.63 L/min), peak airway pressure (–33.04 cmH 2 O), and tidal volume (–312.52 mL) compared with sham ventilation (all p<0.001). In the 24-hour cohort, Sotair was associated with improved oxygenation stability, including higher ABG-derived arterial oxygen saturation at 24 hours compared with sham (+3.34%, p=0.031), lower continuous pulse oximetry-derived oxygen saturation coefficient of variation (1.73% vs 4.26%, p<0.0001), and lower partial pressure carbon dioxide coefficient of variation (12.01% vs 15.29%, p<0.0001). Gross lung injury scores did not differ significantly between treatment groups overall, although injury severity was greater in 24-hour than in 6-hour animals independent of device assignment (p=0.003). Conclusions: Flow modulation using Sotair reduced excessive inspiratory flow, airway pressure, and tidal volume during prolonged manual ventilation while maintaining physiologic stability. Although gross injury outcomes were not significantly different between groups, these findings support further evaluation of Sotair as a low-resource adjunct for prolonged field care and austere settings.
ne71b5cbfd84a: Background: During prehospital airway and ventilatory emergencies including respiratory emergencies, airway compromise, and out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), ventilation delivered by prehospital providers often exceeds recommended airway pressures and ventilation rates. Elevated inspiratory pressures increase intrathoracic pressure, impair venous return, and promote gastric insufflation, increasing the risk of regurgitation and aspiration. Supraglottic airway devices (SGAs) are widely used in emergency medical services because they can be placed rapidly and have high first-pass success rates. However, limited physiologic data describe how SGA design affects esophageal pressure transmission under high-pressure ventilation conditions typical of prehospital resuscitation. Hypothesis: Second-generation SGAs with dual gastric channels will reduce gastric insufflation and distention, reflected by lower esophageal pressures, compared with single-channel devices under conditions simulating cardiac arrest ventilation. Goal: This study compared esophageal pressure transmission and gastric venting among SGAs during pressure-controlled ventilation simulating prehospital cardiac arrest. Methods: In a controlled cadaveric study, fresh unfixed human cadavers were ventilated with multiple SGAs; an endotracheal tube served as the reference standard. Pressure-controlled ventilation was delivered at inspiratory pressures of 20, 30, 40, and 50 cmH 2 O to replicate prehospital ventilation extremes. Distal esophageal pressure was measured continuously through a cannula inserted through the abdominal wall into the stomach and secured in the distal esophagus.
